app.title: New Keynesian Model Lab
app.subtitle: Demand, inflation, interest rates and expectations in the three-equation model (Woodford, Interest and Prices)
app.disclaimer: A teaching model, not a forecast. Textbook calibration (β = 0.99, σ = 1, κ = 0.1, φπ = 1.5, φx = 0.125). The numbers illustrate mechanisms; they do not describe the Czech or any other real economy.

buttons.resetTitle: Return all parameters and the scenario to their default values
buttons.pinTitle: Keep the current curves so you can compare them with another setting

modes.tip: Rational expectations: people know the model and the bank's rule and correctly foresee the future (absent further shocks). Hybrid/adaptive: expectations are formed from the past, Etxt+1 = xt−1 and Etπt+1 = w·π* + (1 − w)·πt−1. Both: the same scenario in both regimes, in one chart.

sizeTip.rn: By how many percentage points (annualized) the natural real rate rⁿ moves: the rate at which demand would exactly match potential. Negative = demand slump (people want to save more, firms invest less).
sizeTip.u: By how many percentage points (annualized) the cost-push shock directly raises inflation in the NKPC, even without overheated demand. Positive = pricier energy or materials, higher markups.
sizeTip.v: By how many percentage points (annualized) the bank sets its rate above what the rule implies. Positive = an unexpected tightening.
sizeTip.istar: By how many percentage points (annualized) the foreign interest rate changes, e.g. the ECB rate. Positive = foreign tightening. Euro deposits pay more, investors move into euros and the koruna depreciates [[UIP]].
sizeTip.ystar: By how many percent of potential foreign demand changes, mainly in the euro area. Negative = a foreign recession. It directly reduces Czech exports [[IS]].
sizeTip.chi: Risk premium: by how many percentage points (annualized) more investors want for holding koruna. Positive = investors sell the koruna and it depreciates [[UIP]]. A premium of +2 p.p. with persistence 0.8 weakens the koruna by roughly 2 to 3%.

shock.rhoTip: How long the shock lasts: each quarter a fraction ρ of last quarter's size remains. ρ = 0.8 is a half-life of about 3 quarters, ρ = 0.95 about 13 quarters. A persistent shock moves expectations more, so its immediate impact is larger.
shock.shapeTip: AR(1): the shock hits fully and fades geometrically. Step: the shock lasts exactly N quarters and then disappears, and everyone knows this in advance (perfect foresight). A step is needed for forward guidance ("after the shock ends").
shock.horizonTip: How many quarters after the shock to display. The rational solution is computed over a longer horizon (at least 60 quarters) so that the terminal condition does not affect the displayed part.

extras.delayTip: For how many quarters after the shock the bank keeps its rate at the neutral level before following the Taylor rule. A delay means the real rate falls while inflation rises, so policy effectively eases.
extras.fg: Promise: keep the rate at the bound N quarters after the shock ends
extras.fgTip: Forward guidance: the bank commits to keep its rate at the lower bound until (end of shock + N), even if the rule would raise it earlier. In the rational regime the promise works through expectations already today. Available only for a "step" shock.
extras.fgNeedsStep: The promise is defined relative to the end of the shock, so it is only available for a "Temporary step" shock.
extras.floor: Exchange-rate commitment: koruna no stronger than
extras.floorTip: In November 2013 the CNB promised not to let the koruna appreciate below 27 CZK/EUR and defended that line by buying euros (interventions). In the model this is a floor for the exchange rate [[UIP]]: whenever the market would want a stronger koruna, the bank intervenes (ξ > 0) and holds the rate exactly at the floor.
extras.commitmentTip: For how many quarters from quarter 1 the bank defends the floor. The actual commitment lasted from November 2013 to April 2017, about 14 quarters. Under rational expectations people foresee its end.

beta.label: β — discount factor
beta.tip: How much firms and households weigh the future (per quarter). β = 0.99 corresponds to a real rate of about 4% p.a. In the Phillips curve it sets how strongly future inflation enters today's prices.

sigma.label: σ — interest sensitivity of demand
sigma.tip: Intertemporal elasticity of substitution: by how many percent demand shifts when the real rate rises by 1 p.p. (per quarter). Large σ = interest rates move spending a lot. Robert Hall (1988) estimated from US data that this sensitivity of consumption is small, closer to 0.1–0.2 than to 1. With a small σ, interest rates (and natural-rate shocks) have a weaker effect on demand.

kappa.label: κ — Phillips-curve slope
kappa.tip: How strongly inflation responds to the output gap. Small κ = very sticky prices (firms reset them rarely); inflation moves little and slowly, and disinflation costs a lot of output. Large κ = more flexible prices.

phiPi.label: φ<sub>π</sub> — rate response to inflation
phiPi.tip: By how much the bank raises the nominal rate when inflation rises by 1 p.p. Taylor principle: it must respond more than one-for-one (roughly φπ > 1) so that the real rate rises with inflation and restrains demand. Below that threshold the model has no unique solution.

phiX.label: φ<sub>x</sub> — rate response to the gap
phiX.tip: By how much the bank raises its rate (quarterly) when output is 1% above potential. 0.125 quarterly corresponds to Taylor's original coefficient of 0.5 in annualized rates.

targetAnn.label: Inflation target π*
targetAnn.tip: The inflation rate the bank aims for (the Czech National Bank targets 2%). In the model it only shifts the displayed levels; the equations work with deviations from target.

neutralRealAnn.label: Neutral real rate r*
neutralRealAnn.tip: The steady-state real rate, with output at potential and inflation at target. Neutral nominal rate = r* + π*. The lower it is, the less room the bank has to cut before it hits the lower bound.

lowerBoundAnn.label: Lower bound on the nominal rate
lowerBoundAnn.tip: The bank will not cut the nominal rate below this level (people would hold cash at a zero return instead). Some banks went slightly below zero, so a negative bound is allowed.

expDiscount.label: m — discounting of expectations
expDiscount.tip: Cognitive discounting (Gabaix 2020): people perceive the distant future in a dampened way. Future output gap and inflation in the IS and NKPC are multiplied by m < 1, so promises about the distant future lose force quickly. m = 1 is the textbook model. Mitigates the forward guidance puzzle. Applies to the rational regime.

anchoring.label: w — anchoring of expectations
anchoring.tip: Hybrid regime: weight of the inflation target in expectations, E<sub>t</sub>π<sub>t+1</sub> = w·π* + (1 − w)·π<sub>t−1</sub>. w = 1: people fully trust the target; w = 0: they expect inflation to be like last quarter's. With endogenous anchoring this is the baseline (maximum) credibility.

endogenousAnchoring.label: Endogenous anchoring
endogenousAnchoring.tip: When on, credibility w falls when inflation stays outside a band around the target for a while, and rebuilds once it returns: w<sub>t+1</sub> = w̄ · exp(−max(0, s<sub>t</sub> − band) / band), where s<sub>t</sub> is a running memory of inflation misses.

anchorBand.label: Tolerance band
anchorBand.tip: How far from target (annualized) inflation may be on average before people start losing trust. The CNB's tolerance band is ±1 p.p.

anchorMemory.label: Memory speed λ
anchorMemory.tip: How fast the latest inflation miss enters the memory s<sub>t</sub> = (1 − λ)s<sub>t−1</sub> + λ|π<sub>t</sub> − π*|. Small λ = people remember long; trust is lost and regained slowly.

alpha.label: α — import share of the consumer basket
alpha.tip: The part of consumer prices that falls on imported goods. The Czech economy is very open, hence the default of 0.35. The higher α, the more the exchange rate moves inflation [[CPI]] and the stronger the exchange-rate channel of monetary policy.

delta.label: δ — response of exports to the exchange rate
delta.tip: By how many percent of potential net exports rise when the koruna depreciates by 1% in real terms [[IS]]. A weaker koruna makes Czech goods cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home, so demand shifts to domestic producers.

gamma.label: γ — response to foreign demand
gamma.tip: By how many percent of potential the Czech output gap changes when the foreign (euro-area) output gap changes by 1% [[IS]]. Exports are a large part of Czech GDP, hence the high γ.

passThrough.label: ψ — speed of exchange-rate pass-through
passThrough.tip: The share of the gap between the exchange rate and import prices that importers close every quarter [[CPI]]. ψ = 1 means immediate and complete pass-through. The default ψ = 0.2 passes a fifth of the remaining gap into import prices each quarter, so a weaker koruna makes imports dearer gradually, as the data show. Fast pass-through (try 0.5 and more) makes the exchange rate a strong but restless channel: a rule that reacts to CPI with a lag starts to oscillate.

fxExpect.label: θ — exchange-rate expectations (hybrid regime)
fxExpect.tip: Hybrid regime: people expect the exchange rate to return towards equilibrium, E<sub>t</sub>q<sub>t+1</sub> = θ·q<sub>t</sub> (regressive expectations, Dornbusch). With θ = 0.8, 80% of today's misalignment is expected to remain next quarter. The higher θ, the more the exchange rate responds to the interest differential [[UIP]]. Under rational expectations the model computes them.

ruleDomestic.label: ω — the bank responds to domestic inflation
ruleDomestic.tip: Which inflation the Taylor rule responds to [[TR]]: 0 = overall consumer (CPI) inflation, 1 = only inflation of domestic goods, i.e. it “looks through” the direct effect of the exchange rate on import prices. Galí and Monacelli (2005) showed that in their model targeting domestic inflation is best. The CNB targeted CPI, but during its exchange-rate commitment it accepted the direct effect of a weaker koruna on prices.

eurCzk.label: Steady-state exchange rate
eurCzk.tip: The koruna exchange rate in the steady state. For display only: the model works with the percentage deviation of the exchange rate. The default of 25.7 CZK/EUR is the rate in autumn 2013, just before the exchange-rate commitment.

charts.components: Inflation of domestic goods and imports

runs.pinsEmpty: Nothing yet. Pin a run, change a parameter and compare the curves.
runs.pinsFull: At most {n} runs can be pinned at once.

status.muc: Solution: method of undetermined coefficients (analytic; AR(1) shock, lower bound not binding).
status.pf: Solution: perfect foresight, one linear system over T = {T} quarters with terminal condition x<sub>T</sub> = π<sub>T</sub> = 0.
status.pfBound: Regimes at the bound found by guess-and-verify ({iter} iterations).
status.forward: Solution: stepping forward; in each quarter the IS, NKPC and the rule with the lower bound are solved simultaneously.
status.nonconv: Regime iteration at the bound did not converge; the result may be unreliable. Try a smaller shock or a shorter promise.
status.unstable: The hybrid path is explosive: with these parameters and adaptive expectations the economy does not stabilize.
status.pfOpen: Solution: perfect foresight for the open economy. One 9T×9T linear system over T = {T} quarters with terminal condition c<sub>T</sub> = π<sup>H</sup><sub>T</sub> = q<sub>T</sub> = 0, solved by banded elimination.
status.forwardOpen: Solution: forward stepping; in every quarter the IS, NKPC, CPI, the exchange rate (UIP) and the rule with the lower bound and the exchange-rate floor are solved simultaneously.

determinacy.title: Rational regime: the model has no unique solution
determinacy.body1: The Taylor principle requires κ(φπ − 1) + (1 − β)φx > 0. Its current value is {v}. Roughly: in response to a permanent 1 p.p. rise in inflation the bank must raise the nominal rate by more than 1 p.p. With these parameters it would need φπ > {th}.
determinacy.body2: Why the solution is not unique without it: when the bank responds weakly, higher expected inflation lowers the real rate i − Etπt+1. Through the IS equation that boosts demand, and through the NKPC it really raises inflation, so expectations fulfil themselves. This works for any (bounded) path of expectations, even without any shock ("sunspots"). The model cannot tell which of infinitely many paths will occur, so we draw none.
determinacy.body3: Technically: the system E<sub>t</sub>z<sub>t+1</sub> = A z<sub>t</sub> for z = (x, π) has two forward-looking variables, and uniqueness requires both eigenvalues of A to lie outside the unit circle. Their moduli are now {eig}.
determinacy.discountNote: With m < 1 the condition changes; the app checks it directly via the eigenvalues.
determinacy.hybridNote: The hybrid regime looks backward, so its solution is unique even here, though not necessarily stable.
determinacy.body3Open: Technically: the open economy has three forward-looking variables (domestic demand, domestic inflation and the real exchange rate) and two predetermined ones (last quarter's exchange rate and the import-price gap). Uniqueness requires three eigenvalues outside the unit circle. One eigenvalue is always exactly 1 (a permanent depreciation offset by lower domestic demand); the long-run condition q → 0 pins it down. Their moduli are now {eig}.

numbers.lossTip: Sum over the displayed horizon of (π − π*)² + 0.5·x², π in % p.a. Smaller = better stabilization. For comparing runs only.

equations.IS: Demand (IS, Hall's Euler equation): today's demand = expected future demand minus σ × (real rate − natural rate).
equations.NKPC: Inflation (New Keynesian Phillips curve): today's inflation = discounted expected inflation + κ × gap + cost-push shock.
equations.TR: Central bank (Taylor rule with a lower bound).
equations.levels: Variables are quarterly deviations from steady state; charts show annualized levels: π in % p.a. = 4π + π*, i in % p.a. = 4i + r* + π*. Shocks are AR(1): z<sub>t</sub> = ρz<sub>t−1</sub>.
equations.CPI: Consumer inflation = (1 − α) × domestic goods + α × imports. Import prices catch up with the exchange rate at speed ψ; Δe is the change of the exchange rate (koruna depreciation = positive).
equations.UIP: Uncovered interest parity: the real exchange rate q (positive = weaker koruna) = the expected rate minus the gap between domestic and foreign real rates, plus the risk premium χ and CNB interventions ξ ≥ 0.
equations.openIS: Demand = domestic demand c (Euler equation) + net exports: a weaker real exchange rate δq and foreign demand γy*.
equations.openNKPC: Inflation of domestic goods: discounted expected domestic inflation + κ × gap + cost-push shock.
equations.openTR: Central bank: Taylor rule with a lower bound. It responds to CPI (ω = 0) or to domestic inflation (ω = 1).
equations.openE: Hybrid expectations (hybrid regime only): inflation and demand from the past; the exchange rate is expected to return towards equilibrium.
equations.levelsOpen: Variables are quarterly deviations from steady state. The charts show annualized levels (π in % p.a. = 4π + π*) and the exchange rate in CZK/EUR = steady-state rate × (1 + e/100), where e = q + p<sup>H</sup> is the nominal exchange rate. Foreign prices are constant.

custom.title: Custom shock
custom.short: Choose the type, size and path of a shock and watch the economy adjust.

oil.title: 1 · Oil/energy shock
oil.short: A cost-push shock: pricier energy raises inflation and lowers output at the same time. The bank has to trade inflation against output.
explain: More expensive energy lowers potential output: the same inputs produce less. In this model it shows up as a cost-push shock u in the [[NKPC]]: firms pass higher costs into prices even though demand is not overheated. (More precisely, u captures the part of the shock by which flexible-price output and efficient output diverge. That divergence is what creates the dilemma.)

The bank's dilemma. The rule [[TR]] with φπ > 1 raises the real rate. Through the [[IS]] that pushes demand below potential (x < 0), and through the κx term in the [[NKPC]] it restrains inflation. Lower inflation is bought with lost output. A cost-push shock breaks the "divine coincidence": no interest rate stabilizes inflation and the gap at the same time.
Dashed: a hawkish bank (φπ = 3). Inflation returns faster and the output loss is deeper. Also try φπ around 1.1: a soft bank keeps inflation high for long but spares output.

Expectations matter too: inflation in the [[NKPC]] depends on E<sub>t</sub>π<sub>t+1</sub>, so a credible commitment to bring inflation back to target dampens it already today. In the hybrid regime high inflation carries over into the following quarters (switch to "Both").

pandemic.title: 2 · Demand collapse (pandemic-type)
pandemic.short: A fall in the natural rate: people want to spend less and save more, firms postpone investment.
explain: Households spend less (caution, closed services) and firms postpone investment. In the model this is a fall in the natural rate rⁿ: the real rate that would keep demand at potential (grey line, bottom right).

[[IS]]: the gap falls as long as the actual real rate is above rⁿ. Iterating forward, x<sub>t</sub> = −σ Σ<sub>k</sub> (r<sub>t+k</sub> − rⁿ<sub>t+k</sub>): today's demand depends on the whole expected path of real rates, not just today's.

Following the [[TR]], the bank cuts its rate, but it reacts only to the fall in inflation and output that has already happened, not to rⁿ directly. The real rate therefore tracks rⁿ only partly and the gap stays negative. If the bank moved its rate exactly with rⁿ, it would stabilize inflation and output at once ("divine coincidence").

[[NKPC]]: a negative gap lowers marginal costs and firms raise prices less, so inflation falls below target. With a demand shock inflation and output move in the same direction, so the bank faces no dilemma.

Dashed: Hall's calibration σ = 0.2. Robert Hall estimated that consumption responds only weakly to the interest rate. With σ = 0.2 both the fall in rⁿ and the bank's response work more weakly through the term σ(r − rⁿ): output moves less, but the bank would need much larger rate moves to influence demand.
A bigger collapse (try −4 p.p.) pushes the rate to the lower bound. That is scenario 3.

zlb.title: 3 · Zero lower bound + forward guidance
zlb.short: A large demand collapse; the rate hits the bound. Does a promise to keep it there after the shock ends help?
explain: The natural rate drops by 5 p.p. for 6 quarters (to −4% p.a.). The rule [[TR]] would want the nominal rate far below zero, but it cannot go below the lower bound. The real rate i − Etπt+1 therefore stays above rⁿ and the [[IS]] sends the economy into a deep recession. Falling expected inflation even raises the real rate at the bound: a deflationary spiral.

Forward guidance: the bank promises to keep the rate at the bound for N more quarters after the shock ends. Why this works is visible in the [[IS]] iterated forward, xt = −σ Σk (it+k − πt+k+1 − rⁿt+k): lower future rates and higher future inflation lower the whole path of real rates, so demand rises already today. The [[NKPC]] adds higher expected inflation, which pushes the real rate at the bound down further.

The forward guidance puzzle. In this model promises are unrealistically powerful. The sum in the [[IS]] has no dampening at all: a promise to cut rates in 5 years moves today's demand as much as a cut today, and the [[NKPC]] adds the whole future boom into today's inflation. Try N = 2 and 4: a few extra quarters of promise turn a deep recession into a boom with high inflation. Empirically, the effects of promises are much smaller (Del Negro, Giannoni and Patterson 2012).

Mitigation: the parameter m (discounting of expectations) in the Advanced section. With m < 1 people perceive the distant future in a dampened way (Gabaix 2020; similarly McKay, Nakamura and Steinsson 2016). In the [[IS]] and [[NKPC]], Etxt+1 and βEtπt+1 are multiplied by m, so the effect of a promise fades geometrically with its horizon. Try m = 0.85.
In the hybrid regime promises do not work through expectations at all, because adaptive expectations only look at the past. What remains is the direct effect of the rate staying low for longer.

deanchor.title: 4 · De-anchoring of expectations
deanchor.short: A cost-push shock, the bank reacts late, and people stop trusting the inflation target.
explain: Hybrid regime: inflation expectations are a weighted average of the target and past inflation [[E]]. The weight w is anchoring, the trust in the target. Endogenous anchoring is on: when inflation stays outside a band around the target for a while, w falls (bottom chart).

After the shock the bank keeps its rate at the neutral level for a few quarters. Expected inflation is rising, so the real rate i − Etπt+1 falls and policy effectively eases. The [[IS]] therefore stimulates demand instead of restraining it.

As w falls, the [[NKPC]] carries more of last quarter's inflation into this quarter's: inflation settles in and starts feeding itself. When the bank finally reacts, it has to raise rates much more and cause a deeper recession, much like the 1970s and the Volcker disinflation.
Dashed: a timely reaction (no delay). Inflation returns to the band, anchoring holds and the loss is smaller. Credibility is capital that is hard to build and easy to lose.

In the rational regime (switch to "Both") the delay hurts too: a fixed rate while inflation rises temporarily violates the Taylor principle, the real rate falls and inflation jumps. But rational agents know the bank will step in later, so inflation does not de-anchor and falls quickly once the bank acts.

koruna.title: 5 · CNB exchange-rate commitment (2013–2017)
koruna.short: Rates at zero, deflation looming. Does promising not to let the koruna appreciate below 27 CZK/EUR help?
explain: Inspired by 2013. Domestic demand weakens, the euro area is in recession (foreign demand −1.5%) and the ECB keeps rates low (−1 p.p.). All three shocks last 10 quarters. Without action (dashed) the rate [[TR]] hits zero, prices fall and the koruna appreciates, because the high real rate and low foreign rates pull capital into koruna [[UIP]]. A stronger koruna makes imports cheaper still [[CPI]] and chokes exports [[IS]].

Exchange-rate commitment: from quarter 1 the bank does not let the koruna appreciate below the chosen floor and defends it with interventions ξ (buying euros). A weaker koruna makes imports dearer, so consumer inflation [[CPI]] moves away from deflation, and supports net exports [[IS]].

Under rational expectations the strongest channel is expectations. The nominal exchange rate cannot fall, so if the koruna is to appreciate in real terms, domestic prices must rise. People therefore expect higher inflation and the real rate at the zero bound falls. The exchange rate is an instrument that still works when rates cannot go lower.

In this scenario the bank responds to domestic inflation (ω = 1), just as the CNB accepted the direct effect of a weaker koruna on prices. Try ω = 0: the rule then answers imported inflation by raising the rate and undermines the commitment itself.

The exit: the market knows the koruna will appreciate once the commitment ends, and money pours in just before the end. Interventions shoot up, as in spring 2017. After the exit the koruna appreciates, because the floor held it weaker than equilibrium.

In the hybrid regime there is no expectations channel and the commitment helps only mechanically, through import prices and exports. It does little for output and the jump in the exchange rate rather unsettles inflation, so the loss can even come out higher. The power of an exchange-rate commitment rests mainly on credibility and expectations.

rn: The natural rate rⁿ is the real rate at which demand would exactly match potential. When it falls (people want to save more, firms invest less), the prevailing real rate is suddenly too high.

[[IS]]: the output gap falls when the real rate i − E<sub>t</sub>π<sub>t+1</sub> is above rⁿ. Iterating forward, x<sub>t</sub> = −σ Σ<sub>k</sub>(r<sub>t+k</sub> − rⁿ<sub>t+k</sub>): the whole expected path of real rates matters.

[[NKPC]]: weaker demand means lower marginal costs, so firms that get to reset prices raise them less and inflation falls. Inflation is forward-looking: π<sub>t</sub> = κ Σ<sub>k</sub> β<sup>k</sup> x<sub>t+k</sub>.
[[TR]]: the bank cuts its rate, but it reacts only to π and x, not to rⁿ directly. The real rate therefore falls less than the natural rate and the gap stays negative.
u: A cost-push shock u shifts the Phillips curve [[NKPC]] up: inflation rises even with a zero gap (pricier inputs, higher markups).

Following the [[TR]] the bank raises its rate by more than inflation (φ<sub>π</sub> > 1), the real rate rises and through the [[IS]] restrains demand. The negative gap then slows inflation through κx in the [[NKPC]].
The bank thus trades some inflation for lost output. With a cost-push shock you cannot stabilize both at once. Try changing φ<sub>π</sub> and comparing pinned runs.
v: A monetary shock v is a deviation from the rule [[TR]]: the bank sets its rate higher than the rule implies.
Prices are sticky, so a higher nominal rate means a higher real rate. Demand falls in the [[IS]] and inflation falls in the [[NKPC]].

The rule then undoes part of the tightening by itself: lower π and x pull the rate down. Under the default calibration the nominal rate actually falls while the real rate rises. Policy is measured by the path of the real rate, not the nominal one.
istar: The foreign interest rate i* rises, for example when the ECB tightens. With an unchanged Czech rate it pays to hold euros, investors sell the koruna and it weakens. This is uncovered interest parity [[UIP]]: the real exchange rate equals the sum of future real-rate differentials.
A weaker koruna makes imports dearer, so consumer inflation [[CPI]] rises, and makes Czech exports cheaper, so demand [[IS]] gets a short-run boost.

Following its rule [[TR]], the bank answers higher inflation by raising its rate, which undoes part of the depreciation. A small open economy thus imports monetary policy from abroad: when the ECB tightens, the CNB has to tighten a little too.
ystar: Foreign demand falls, typically in a euro-area recession. Czech exports fall directly, so the output gap falls [[IS]] and so does domestic inflation [[NKPC]].

The bank cuts its rate under the [[TR]] and the koruna weakens [[UIP]]. That cushions the fall: a weaker koruna supports exports and makes imports dearer, so consumer inflation [[CPI]] falls less than domestic inflation. In the hybrid regime CPI can even rise for a moment.
A floating exchange rate works as an automatic stabilizer here. Try γ = 0: the foreign recession then leaves the economy untouched.
chi: Exchange-rate shock: investors suddenly want a higher return for holding koruna (risk premium χ), say because of regional uncertainty. With unchanged rates the koruna depreciates at once [[UIP]].

Imports get dearer and consumer inflation [[CPI]] jumps even though domestic demand is not overheating. For the bank it is like a cost-push shock: raising the rate [[TR]] supports the koruna and dampens inflation, at the price of weaker demand [[IS]].
Try ω = 1 in the Open economy section: the bank then looks through the direct effect of the exchange rate on prices and lets imported inflation fade on its own.

mode.hybrid: Hybrid regime: expectations are formed from the past [[E]]. Responses are therefore slower and hump-shaped (the peak comes several quarters later) and promises about the future have no effect. The discounting parameter m does not apply in this regime.
mode.both: Comparing regimes: blue = rational expectations, orange = hybrid. The difference shows how much work expectations do in the model.
mode.open: Open economy: besides demand [[IS]], the rate also works through the koruna [[UIP]]. A higher rate strengthens the koruna, imports get cheaper and consumer inflation [[CPI]] falls faster than in the closed economy; a stronger koruna also dampens net exports.

note.bound: The rate is at the lower bound ({lb}% p.a.) in quarters {list} (shading in the nominal-rate chart). There the rule [[TR]] does not apply and only higher expected inflation can lower the real rate.
note.delay: The bank reacts with a delay of {n} qtrs: until then it keeps its rate at the neutral level regardless of the [[TR]].
note.discount: Discounting of expectations m = {m}: future values in the [[IS]] and [[NKPC]] are dampened.
note.floor: The koruna is at the commitment floor ({floor} CZK/EUR) in quarters {list} (shading in the exchange-rate chart). There the bank intervenes: it buys euros so that the koruna is not stronger [[UIP]].

live.title: Live diagram: who drives whom

intro.rational: Each arrow shows how much one term of an equation contributes to the variable it points to in the selected quarter. The arrows entering a node add up exactly to its value: demand by the [[IS]], inflation by the [[NKPC]], the rate by the [[TR]]. Under rational expectations, expectations look ahead: E<sub>t</sub>x<sub>t+1</sub> and E<sub>t</sub>π<sub>t+1</sub> are next quarter's values, so the future acts today. Play, step through or drag the timeline above; hovering over a chart moves it too.
intro.hybrid: Each arrow shows how much one term of an equation contributes to the variable it points to in the selected quarter. The arrows entering a node add up exactly to its value: demand by the [[IS]], inflation by the [[NKPC]], the rate by the [[TR]]. Under hybrid expectations, expectations are formed from the past [[E]]: E<sub>t</sub>x<sub>t+1</sub> = x<sub>t−1</sub> and E<sub>t</sub>π<sub>t+1</sub> = (1 − w)·π<sub>t−1</sub> (as deviations from target), which is why responses come with a lag. Play, step through or drag the timeline; hovering over a chart moves it too.

legendInfo.hybrid: where expectations come from (the past, t−1)

live.legendWidth: Arrow width and pulse speed are proportional to the size of the contribution, on one scale for the whole period. The gap is in % of potential, inflation and the rate in p.p. p.a. relative to the target and to the neutral rate.

live.calm: No term plays a big role right now.
live.introOpen: In the open economy there is one more node, the Koruna exchange rate [[UIP]]: the rate and expectations move it, and it acts on inflation through import prices [[CPI]] and on demand through net exports (the arc over the top) [[IS]]. Foreign shocks i*, χ and y* come in from outside.

nodeTips.exp_rational: Expected gap and inflation next quarter. Under rational expectations they equal next quarter's actual values.
nodeTips.exp_hybrid: Expected gap and inflation next quarter. Under hybrid expectations they are formed from last quarter; w is the credibility of the inflation target.
nodeTips.demand: Output gap x: demand relative to potential (IS).
nodeTips.bank: Nominal rate i and real rate i − Eπ in % p.a. (Taylor rule with a lower bound).
nodeTips.fx_rational: The koruna in CZK/EUR and the real exchange rate q (positive = weaker koruna). Rational investors know the future path of the exchange rate (UIP).
nodeTips.fx_hybrid: The koruna in CZK/EUR and the real exchange rate q (positive = weaker koruna). In the hybrid regime investors expect the rate to return gradually towards equilibrium, E q = θ q.
nodeTips.demand_open: Output gap x = domestic demand + net exports (IS).
nodeTips.inflation_open: Consumer (CPI) inflation in % p.a. = domestic goods + imports.

arrows.expDemand: m·E x + σ·E π: when people expect higher demand they spend today; higher expected inflation lowers the real rate (IS).
arrows.bankDemand: −σ·i: a higher nominal rate, for given expectations, raises the real rate and slows demand (IS). Feedback from the bank.
arrows.shockDemand: σ·rⁿ: the natural rate, i.e. a demand shock (IS).
arrows.expInfl: β·m·E π: firms that reset prices now take expected inflation into account (NKPC).
arrows.demandInfl: κ·x: higher demand raises marginal costs and firms raise prices (NKPC).
arrows.shockInfl: u: a cost-push shock, such as more expensive energy (NKPC).
arrows.inflBank: φπ·π: the bank responds to inflation (TR).
arrows.demandBank: φx·x: the bank responds to the output gap (TR).
arrows.shockBank: v: a monetary shock, the bank deviating from its rule (TR).
arrows.limitBank: Difference between the actual rate and the rule: the lower bound (the rate cannot go lower), a delayed response, a promise (forward guidance), in the game the player's decision.
arrows.expDemand_open: m·E c + σ·E πᴴ: expected domestic demand and expected inflation (lowers the real rate) (IS).
arrows.expInfl_open: (1 − α)·β·m·E πᴴ: expected inflation in the prices of domestic goods (NKPC, CPI).
arrows.demandInfl_open: (1 − α)·κ·x: higher demand raises the prices of domestic goods (NKPC, CPI).
arrows.shockInfl_open: (1 − α)·u: a cost-push shock in domestic prices (NKPC, CPI).
arrows.expFx: E q + E πᴴ: the expected future exchange rate and expected inflation, which lowers the domestic real rate (UIP).
arrows.bankFx: −i: a higher domestic rate attracts capital and strengthens the koruna (UIP).
arrows.interveneFx: ξ: bank interventions (buying euros) that hold the koruna at the commitment floor (UIP).
arrows.fxInfl: α·πᶠ: a weaker koruna makes imports dearer and lifts consumer inflation (CPI).
arrows.fxDemand: δ·q: a weaker koruna makes exports cheaper and imports dearer, net exports rise (IS).
arrows.foreignFx: i*: a higher foreign rate draws capital away and weakens the koruna (UIP).
arrows.shockFx: χ: the risk premium investors want for holding koruna (UIP).
arrows.foreignDemand: γ·y*: foreign demand for Czech exports (IS).

infoTitle.rational: Rational expectations: people know the model, so they expect what will actually happen next quarter.
infoTitle.hybrid: Hybrid expectations: the forecast is formed from last quarter.

game.title: Be the central bank
game.lead: You are the bank board. Every quarter you set the nominal interest rate and try to keep inflation at the 2% target without needless swings in output. Random shocks hit the economy along the way.
rules: You move the rate in steps of 0.25 p.p. It cannot go below the lower bound (0%).
You see the data with a one-quarter lag, and they are noisy first estimates. The output gap is much harder to measure than inflation.
Expectations are hybrid [[E]]: people look at the past and trust the target with weight w. Credibility grows while inflation stays within ±1 p.p. of the target and falls when it gets away.
News about big events (energy prices, a collapse in demand) arrives at once, but without numbers.
If inflation gets more than 10 p.p. away from the target or the output gap beyond ±12%, the government replaces you and the game ends early.
No score is shown during the game. After the last quarter you get a review and a comparison with the autopilot.
game.lengthTip: Number of quarters you decide (default 24 = 6 years). They are preceded by 4 quarters of history in which the bank followed the Taylor rule.
game.difficultyTip: Difficulty scales the demand and cost shocks (mild ×{easy}, hard ×{hard}). The noise in the data stays the same. On hard, the rate hits the lower bound more often, and occasionally the economy can fall into a deflation trap.
game.seedTip: The same seed gives the same sequence of shocks and of data noise. You can replay a game with another strategy or pass the number on to someone else. The default, 1998, is the year the Czech National Bank switched to inflation targeting.
explain: Why hybrid expectations. Rational expectations in the [[IS]] and [[NKPC]] assume that people know the rule the bank follows. A player has no fixed rule and decides quarter by quarter. That is why expectations in the game are formed from the past [[E]].

Credibility is capital. The weight w of the target in expectations starts at 0.6. While inflation stays within the band it grows towards 0.9; when inflation stays outside for long, it falls. With weak credibility, last year's inflation feeds more into this year's [[NKPC]] and every shock lasts longer.
Demand accumulates. With Etxt+1 = xt−1, the output gap in the [[IS]] keeps moving as long as the real rate differs from the natural rate. Doing nothing lets the gap drift quarter after quarter.

Lagged, noisy data. You decide on last quarter's figures, and they can be wrong. React to every wiggle and you react to noise; wait too long and you react late. The rule [[TR]] is a useful guide, but in the game nobody applies it for you.
game.lossNote: Loss = Σ [(π − π*)² + {wg}·x² + {wr}·(Δi)²] over your quarters; π and i in % p.a., x in % of potential, Δi is the change of the rate from the previous quarter. Lower is better.
game.observedNote: The charts show only what the bank knows: first estimates with measurement error (noise standard deviation: inflation {gi} p.p., gap {gx}%). The grey strip is the history before you took over.

charts.histNote: grey strip = history before you took over

news.rn_up: Firms report record orders and households are spending more.
news.rn_down: Firms are cancelling investment and households start saving.
news.u_up: Energy and commodity prices are surging.
news.u_down: Energy and commodity prices are tumbling.
news.ystar_up: The euro area grows faster than expected and demand for Czech exports rises.
news.ystar_down: The euro area slows down and foreign customers cancel orders.
news.chi_up: Investors flee the region and sell the koruna.
news.chi_down: Foreign capital is flowing into the koruna.

game.keys: Keys: ↑ / ↓ move the rate by 0.25 p.p. (by 1 with Shift), Enter confirms.

verdict.lost: The economy got out of control: inflation ran far away from the target. Your loss {p}, autopilot {a}.
verdict.better: Better than the autopilot! Your loss {p}, autopilot {a}.
verdict.close: Almost as good as the autopilot: your loss {p}, autopilot {a}.
verdict.worse: The autopilot did better: your loss {p}, autopilot {a}.
verdict.muchWorse: The autopilot did much better: your loss {p}, autopilot {a}.
verdict.beatData: Applied to the same noisy data you saw, the same rule had a loss of {d}, so your decisions were better.
verdict.lostData: Applied to the same noisy data you saw, the same rule had a loss of {d}.
verdict.firedLoss: Over the same quarters: your loss {p}, autopilot {a}.

late.high: The data showed inflation of {infl}% p.a., above the tolerance band, yet the rate stayed around {rate}% for {n} qtrs. The Taylor rule would have set about {rule}% on the same data. When inflation rises and the nominal rate stands still, the real rate falls: policy was in effect easing [[IS]] and high inflation was spilling into expectations [[E]].
late.low: The data showed inflation of {infl}% p.a., below the tolerance band, yet the rate stayed around {rate}% for {n} qtrs. The rule would have set about {rule}% on the same data. Too high a real rate held demand down [[IS]] and low inflation undermined trust in the target [[E]].

over.up_inflation: Raising the rate by {move} p.p. to {rate}% went far beyond what the data suggested (rule about {rule}%). In {at} inflation then fell to {value}%, below the tolerance band. The rate works with a lag through demand [[IS]] and the [[NKPC]], so a big jump overshoots.
over.up_gap: Raising the rate by {move} p.p. to {rate}% went far beyond what the data suggested (rule about {rule}%). In {at} the output gap then fell to {value}%: a needlessly deep slump [[IS]].
over.down_inflation: Cutting the rate by {move} p.p. to {rate}% went far beyond what the data suggested (rule about {rule}%). In {at} inflation then jumped to {value}%, above the tolerance band [[NKPC]].
over.down_gap: Cutting the rate by {move} p.p. to {rate}% went far beyond what the data suggested (rule about {rule}%). In {at} the output gap then rose to {value}%: overheating [[IS]].

noise.up_gap: Raising the rate by {move} p.p. followed a strong output-gap reading ({seen}%). The actual gap was {truth}%: most of the signal was measurement noise. The gap is much harder to measure than inflation, so it pays to wait for confirmation in later data.
noise.down_gap: Cutting the rate by {move} p.p. followed a weak output-gap reading ({seen}%). The actual gap was {truth}%: most of the signal was measurement noise. The gap is much harder to measure than inflation, so it pays to wait for confirmation in later data.
noise.up_inflation: Raising the rate by {move} p.p. followed a high inflation reading ({seen}%). Actual inflation was {truth}%: much of the signal was measurement noise. One reading does not make a trend.
noise.down_inflation: Cutting the rate by {move} p.p. followed a low inflation reading ({seen}%). Actual inflation was {truth}%: much of the signal was measurement noise. One reading does not make a trend.

supply.down: A cost-push shock was lifting inflation (u ≈ +{cost} p.p.), yet the rate was cut by {cut} p.p. to {rate}%, probably because output was weaker (gap in the data {gap}%). Inflation was already above target ({infl}%). The lower real rate added demand and gave inflation in the [[NKPC]] more fuel. With a cost-push shock the bank has to accept a temporary fall in output.
supply.credibility: Credibility of the target fell from {w0} to {w1} [[E]].

game.costTip: How much higher your loss was than the autopilot's in this quarter and the following {n}.

facts.credibility: Credibility of the target w: {w0} at the start, {w1} at the end, lowest {wmin} (autopilot at the end {wa}).
facts.moves: The rate changed in {n} of {N} quarters, by {m} p.p. on average (autopilot {na}×, by {ma} p.p. on average).
facts.worst: Inflation was furthest from target in {q}: {v}% p.a.

game.autopilotNote: The autopilot follows the model's Taylor rule and sees the current quarter's actual data, so it has an information advantage. The row “Rule on your data” applies the same rule to the same lagged, noisy data that you see.
game.noMistakes: None of the mistakes we look for (late reaction, overreaction, reacting to noise, easing in a supply shock) cost anything substantial. Well done.
game.rulesNote: The review is generated by fixed rules from the game data (the thresholds are listed in the README), not by a language model. Mistakes are sorted by how much they cost.

fired.inflation: The government replaced you in {q}: inflation shot up to {v}% p.a. Only the quarters played are reviewed (out of {n} planned).
fired.deflation: The government replaced you in {q}: inflation fell to {v}% p.a. and the economy is sliding into deflation. Only the quarters played are reviewed (out of {n} planned).
fired.boom: The government replaced you in {q}: the economy overheated, output gap {v}%. Only the quarters played are reviewed (out of {n} planned).
fired.slump: The government replaced you in {q}: a deep recession, output gap {v}%. Only the quarters played are reviewed (out of {n} planned).

game.economyTip: The closed economy as in phase 2, or a small open economy with the koruna exchange rate [[UIP]]. In the open economy the rate moves the koruna in the same quarter; the exchange rate then feeds gradually into import prices [[CPI]] and into exports [[IS]]. Foreign shocks are added: euro-area demand, the ECB rate and investor sentiment towards the koruna. You see the exchange rate at once and exactly, because it is a market price.

economy.label: Economy
economy.tip: Closed: the three-equation model of phase 1, unchanged. Open: a small open economy like Czechia. It adds the koruna exchange rate (uncovered interest parity [[UIP]]), imports in the consumer price basket [[CPI]], net exports in demand [[IS]] and foreign shocks: the foreign interest rate, foreign demand and an exchange-rate shock. Without trade (α = δ = γ = 0) the open model gives exactly the same results as the closed one.
